<div class="game-page">
<div class="game-head">
<div class="game-meta">game</div>
<div class="game-subtitle">With four back-games; two from the 4th, one from the 9th, and the last from the 11th move.</div>
<hr class="game-rule">
</div>
<div class="philidor-game">
<div class="game-board">
<div class="pgn-board"><script type="text/pgn">[Event "Philidor, Analysis of the Game of Chess (London, 1777)"]
[Site "?"]
[Date "1777.??.??"]
[Round "-"]
[White "Philidor (analysis)"]
[Black "Philidor (analysis)"]
[Result "*"]
[Annotator "F. D. Philidor"]
[PhilidorGame "Second Gambit"]
[PhilidorKind "game"]
[SourceLine "2878"]

1. e4 {The king's pawn, two moves.} e5 {The same.} 2. f4 {The king's bishop's pawn, two moves.}
exf4 {The pawn takes the pawn.} 3. Bc4 {The king's bishop, at his queen's bishop's fourth
square.} Qh4+ {The queen gives check.} 4. Kf1 {The king, at his bishop's square.} g5 {The king's
knight's pawn, two moves. (a) NOTE: There are two other different ways of playing this move: the
first is, to play his king's bishop to his queen's bishop's fourth square; and the other, to
push that queen's same pawn one move, which will make the subject of two back-games.} 5. Nf3
{The king's knight, at his bishop's third square.} Qh5 {The queen, at her king's rook's fourth
square. (b) NOTE: He might have removed his queen to two other squares; but this is the best:
for, had he made her retire to your king's knight's fourth square, you might have taken his
king's bishop's pawn, by giving check, and perhaps afterwards forced his queen: and, if he had
withdrawn her to his king's rook's third square, you must have attacked the same king's bishop's
pawn with your king's knight, which would have entirely decided the game in your favour.} 6. d4
{The queen's pawn, two moves.} d6 {The queen's pawn, one move.} 7. c3 {The queen's bishop's
pawn, one move. (c) NOTE: It is of consequence, in the gambits, to play this pawn, to enable
yourself afterwards to place your queen at her knight's third square. In this post, that
increases the strength of your position, and perplexes your adversary, especially if he has
played his queen's bishop, without attacking one of your pieces. See, respecting this play, the
fifth and sixth back-games of the first gambit.} Bg4 {The queen's bishop, at the adverse king's
knight's fourth square.} 8. Kf2 {The king, at his bishop's second square.} Nf6 {The king's
knight, at his king's bishop's third square. (d) NOTE: If, instead of playing this knight, he
had taken your king's knight, a third backgame will show you how you are to proceed in that
party.} 9. Qe2 {The queen, at her king's second square.} Nbd7 {The queen's knight, at his
queen's second square.} 10. h4 {The king's rook's pawn, two moves.} Bxf3 {The bishop takes the
knight.} 11. Qxf3 {The queen takes the bishop.} Qxf3+ {The queen takes the queen. (e) NOTE: If,
instead of taking your queen, he had given check, a fourth back-game will show you how he would
lose the game.} 12. Kxf3 {The king retakes the queen. (f) NOTE: I have laid it down, as a
general rule, always to unite your pawns, and bring them into the centre. Here is however an
exception, grounded upon two good reasons: first, if you retake with your king, you gain a pawn,
your adversary being no longer able to hinder it: secondly, the queen being changed, your king
has nothing to fear; and getting him into action, he may be as useful to you as any other of
your pieces.} g4+ {The king's knight's pawn gives check.} 13. Kxf4 {The king takes the adverse
king's pawn.} Bh6+ {The king's bishop gives check at the rook's third square.} 14. Kf5 {The
king, at the adverse king's bishop's fourth square. (g) NOTE: Your king could not be safe on
that square, if your adversary had yet a white bishop to dislodge him from that post; but, this
not being the case, your king sustains all your pawns.} Bxc1 {The king's bishop takes the
adverse queen's bishop.} 15. Rxc1 {The king's rook takes the bishop.} h5 {The king's rook's
pawn, two moves.} 16. Nd2 {The knight, at his queen's second square.} Ke7 {The king, at his
second square.} 17. Rf1 {The king's rook, at its king's bishop's square. (h) NOTE: You might
have played this rook to your king's square; but in this case your queen's rook would have been
almost useless to you: it is better then to retard your attack, and get all your pieces into
action.} c6 {The queen's bishop's pawn, one move. (i) NOTE: He prepares to push his queen's pawn
one move, to break your centre; which it behoves you to prevent, by putting him under the
necessity of defending himself.} 18. Rae1 {The queen's rook, at its king's square.} b5 {The
queen's knight's pawn, two moves. (k) NOTE: He endeavours to attack you on your left, and make
an opening for his rooks.} 19. Bb3 {The bishop, at his queen's knight's third square.} a5 {The
queen's rook's pawn, two moves.} 20. e5 {The king's pawn, one move.} dxe5 {The pawn takes the
pawn.} 21. dxe5 {The queen's pawn retakes the pawn.} Nd5 {The king's knight, at his queen's
fourth square.} 22. Ne4 {The knight, at his king's fourth square. (l) NOTE: You would have
played very ill in taking his knight with your bishop; because, by retaking your bishop with his
pawn, this very pawn would obstruct the passage of your knight: it was necessary then to play
this knight first, in order to have no useless pieces.} N7b6 {The queen's knight, at his third
square.} 23. Nf6 {The knight, at the adverse king's bishop's third square.} Rad8 {The queen's
rook, at its queen's square. (m) NOTE: If he had taken your knight, you should have retaken with
the pawn, and afterwards attacked his king's bishop's pawn, by playing your queen's rook to its
king's second square.} 24. e6 {The king's pawn, one move.} Rd6 {The queen's rook, at its queen's
third square. (n) NOTE: If, instead of playing the rook, he had taken your pawn, you would have
won the game in a few moves, because he would lose his queen's bishop's pawn; as, if he had
taken your knight with his own, you would have taken his pawn with your's, in giving check, by
discovery.} 25. exf7+ {The pawn takes the pawn, and gives check with the rook.} Kxf7 {The king
takes the pawn.} 26. Kg5 {The king, at the adverse king's knight's fourth square.} Kg7 {The
king, at his knight's second square, to avoid a check by discovery.} 27. Nxh5+ {The knight takes
the king's rook's pawn, and gives check.} Kh7 {The king, at his rook's second square.} 28. Rf7+
{The king's rook gives check.} Kg8 {The king, at his knight's square.} 29. Rb7 {The king's rook,
at the adverse queen's knight's second square.} Rd8 {The queen's rook, at its queen's square.
(o) NOTE: If he had played his king instead of his queen's rook, you could have given check with
your queen's rook, and taken that of his king. It is convenient to observe here, that what has
decided the game in favour of the white, is, that the king, having been in a situation fit for
action, has been as useful as the best of his pieces.} 30. Rxb6 {The rook takes the adverse
queen's knight, and wins the game in course.} *
</script></div>
